questions.stem: An adjacency matrix for a graph with V vertices and E edges uses memory:
questions.explanation: A V × V grid, whatever E is. O(V + E) (a) is the adjacency list.

questions.stem: Breadth-first search keeps the vertices waiting to be expanded in a:
questions.explanation: First discovered, first expanded. A stack (b) gives DFS; a priority queue (c) gives Dijkstra's algorithm, beyond this course.

questions.stem: An undirected graph has 7 vertices with degrees 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3 and 1. How many edges does it have?
questions.explanation: The degrees add up to 2 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 16, and every edge is counted at both ends: E = 16 / 2 = 8. 16 (a) forgets to halve. (These are the degrees of H.)

questions.stem: BFS from s always reaches a vertex first along a path with the fewest edges because:
options: the queue releases vertices in order of non-decreasing distance from s
it marks vertices when they are dequeued
it tries every path and keeps the shortest
questions.explanation: The queue holds all of distance d before any of distance d + 1, so a vertex is discovered while BFS is expanding the layer just before it. It never tries every path (c) — that would be exponential. Marking on dequeue (b) is a bug (W14-B1).

questions.stem: bfs(H, "A") returns:
options: A B C D E F G
A B D C E F G
A B C F E D G
A D B E C F G
questions.explanation: A adds B and D; B adds C and E; D adds nothing new; C adds F; F adds G (W14-T1). (a) is alphabetical order, which BFS does not use.

questions.stem: dfs(H, "A") returns:
options: A B D C E F G
A B C E F D G
A B C F E D G
A D E B C F G
questions.explanation: A → B → C → F → E → D, back up to F, then G (W14-T2). (a) is what you get if you think of BFS layers; (b) goes from C to E, but C and E are not adjacent.

questions.stem: shortest_path_unweighted(H, "D", "C") returns:
questions.explanation: D's list is A, E, so A is taken first and becomes B's parent; B then discovers C. D–E–B–C (c) and D–E–F–C (a) are also three edges long — equally short — but BFS keeps the first parent it records (W14-T4).

questions.stem: has_edge(u, v) on an adjacency matrix costs:
questions.explanation: One cell, matrix[i][j], after two O(1) hash-map lookups for i and j. O(deg u) (b) is the list.

questions.stem: neighbours(u) on an adjacency matrix costs:
questions.explanation: The whole row of V cells must be scanned to find the 1s. That is the matrix's price.

questions.stem: A BFS on a MatrixGraph costs O(V2) even when the graph has very few edges, because:
options: finding each vertex's neighbours scans its whole row of V cells
every cell of the matrix is hashed
the visited set is a matrix too
questions.explanation: V vertices, each costing a V-cell row scan: V2. The number of edges does not change the work.

questions.stem: An undirected graph with E edges is stored as an adjacency list. How many neighbour entries do the lists hold in total?
questions.explanation: Each undirected edge u–v is stored in u's list and in v's list. The same fact is Σ deg(v) = 2E.

questions.stem: BFS marks a vertex as visited when it is enqueued, not when it is dequeued, because otherwise:
options: a vertex can be put in the queue more than once
BFS would miss some reachable vertices
the search would no longer find shortest paths
questions.explanation: A vertex with two neighbours that are taken before it is enqueued by both, and then appears twice in the order (W14-B1). BFS still finds every vertex (b) — it just repeats some.

questions.stem: dfs_iterative pushes each vertex's neighbours in reverse order because:
options: a stack is first in, first out
the first neighbour must come off the stack first, to match dfs
otherwise the search never ends on a cycle
questions.explanation: A stack is last in, first out (not a): pushing D then B from A's list B, D puts B on top, so B comes off first — the same choice the recursive for loop makes.

questions.stem: The recursive dfs is run on a graph that is one path of 5,000 vertices. In Python, with the default settings, it:
questions.explanation: One call frame per vertex on the path; Python's default limit is 1,000 frames. The reference dfs already fails on a path of 1,000 edges. dfs_iterative handles it.

questions.stem: A DAG is:
options: a connected undirected graph with no cycle
a graph whose every vertex has the same degree
a graph stored as a matrix
a directed graph with no cycle
questions.explanation: Directed acyclic graph. (a) describes a tree.

questions.stem: topological_sort on the directed graph A → B, B → C, C → A returns:
questions.explanation: Every vertex keeps in-degree 1, so the ready queue starts empty, nothing is output, and 0 < 3 vertices means a cycle: None. The ValueError (d) is for an undirected graph.

questions.stem: Undirected cycle detection ignores a visited neighbour that is the vertex's parent, because:
options: every undirected edge is stored in both lists, so the vertex you came from always looks visited
a parent cannot be part of a cycle
it makes the search O(V + E)
questions.explanation: When DFS enters B from A, B's list contains A. Without the check every edge would be reported as a cycle (W14-B3).

questions.stem: In the directed diamond A → B, A → C, B → D, C → D, a DFS from A meets D a second time, from C. That is not a cycle, because at that moment D is:
questions.explanation: D was finished when the search backed up from B; it is no longer on the current path A → C. Only an edge to a grey vertex (b) closes a cycle.

questions.stem: A graph has vertices A to I and the undirected edges A–B, B–C, D–E, F–G. How many connected components does it have?
questions.explanation: {A, B, C}, {D, E}, {F, G}, and H and I on their own. A vertex with no edges is a component of its own; 4 (a) and 3 (b) forget H and I.

questions.stem: topological_sort(P) returns:
options: A B C D E F
B D A C E F
A C B D E F
F E D C B A
questions.explanation: In-degree 0 at the start: A and B, queued in node order. A releases nothing (C still waits on B); B releases C and D; C, then D, then E, then F (W14-T5). (b) is also a valid topological order — it is the DFS one — but it is not what Kahn's algorithm returns. (c) puts C before B, although B → C.

questions.stem: Which of these can BFS on its own not answer correctly?
options: the path with the fewest edges from s to t
whether t can be reached from s
the shortest route by kilometres on a road map with different road lengths
the connected components of an undirected graph
questions.explanation: BFS counts edges; with road lengths the fewest roads is not the fewest kilometres. That needs Dijkstra's algorithm, which this course only names.

questions.stem: One BFS over an adjacency list costs:
questions.explanation: Every vertex is enqueued and dequeued once; every list is read once, Σ deg = 2E entries in total.
